subject: biology
title: A1.1 Water
welcome_lead: Today's adventure: A1.1 Water — IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025), topic A1.1.
meta_desc: IB DP Biology practice covering A1.1 Water, guide topic A1.1.
final_note: You worked through A1.1 Water — 8 guide statements.

concepts.term: Water as the medium for life
concepts.def: The first cells originated in water, and water remains the medium in which most of the processes of life take place: the cytoplasm of every cell is an aqueous solution in which metabolic reactions occur, and substances are transported dissolved in water. This is as true of organisms living on land or in the air as of aquatic organisms, because their cells carry water inside them.

A covalent bond in which the shared pair of electrons is drawn unequally towards one of the two atoms. In water, the oxygen atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than each hydrogen atom, so the oxygen carries a partial negative charge (δ−) and each hydrogen a partial positive charge (δ+). The water molecule as a whole is therefore polar.

The notation used to show polarity when representing water molecules: δ− (delta minus) is written beside the oxygen atom and δ+ (delta plus) beside each hydrogen atom. A hydrogen bond between molecules is shown as a dashed line joining a δ+ hydrogen of one molecule to the δ− oxygen of a neighbouring molecule. The δ symbol indicates a partial charge, much smaller than the full charge of an ion.

An attraction between molecules (an intermolecular force) in which a δ+ hydrogen atom that is covalently bonded to a strongly electronegative atom is attracted to a δ− atom of a neighbouring molecule. In water, hydrogen bonds form between the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule and the δ− oxygen of another; each water molecule can form up to four. An individual hydrogen bond is weak compared with a covalent bond and, in liquid water, hydrogen bonds continually break and re-form, but the very large number present gives water its cohesive, adhesive, solvent and thermal properties.

The attraction between molecules of the same substance. Water molecules cohere because of the hydrogen bonds between them. Cohesion allows water to be pulled up xylem vessels as a continuous column under tension and gives the surface of water a high surface tension.

The effect that makes the surface of a liquid behave like a stretched elastic film. Water molecules at the surface are pulled by hydrogen bonds to the molecules beside and beneath them, but not by the air above, so the surface resists being broken. Water's surface tension is high enough for small animals such as pond skaters to stand and move on the surface, so the water surface can be used as a habitat.

concepts.term: Transport of water under tension in xylem
concepts.def: Tension is a pulling force (a pressure below atmospheric). Evaporation of water from the cell walls of leaf cells during transpiration draws water out of the xylem, placing the column of water in each xylem vessel under tension. Because hydrogen bonds hold the water molecules together (cohesion), the tension is transmitted down the continuous column, so water is pulled up from the roots without the column breaking.

The attraction between water molecules and molecules of a different substance. Water adheres to surfaces that are polar or charged, because the δ+ and δ− parts of water molecules are attracted to charges or partial charges on the surface (for example, by hydrogen bonding to the hydroxyl groups of cellulose). Water does not adhere to non-polar surfaces such as the wax of a leaf cuticle.

The movement of water through narrow spaces, including against gravity, caused by adhesion of water to the polar or charged walls of the spaces together with cohesion between the water molecules. Capillary action moves water through the narrow spaces between soil particles, making it available to roots, and through the spaces between cellulose fibres in plant cell walls; in a leaf, water drawn into cell walls by capillary action replaces the water that evaporates from them.

Describes a substance that is attracted to water and dissolves in it (or, if solid, is wetted by it) because its molecules are polar or carry charges, so that water molecules form hydrogen bonds with them or are attracted to their charges. Glucose, amino acids, sodium chloride and most proteins are hydrophilic. Because a wide variety of hydrophilic substances dissolve in water, water is the medium for metabolism (most enzymes catalyse reactions in aqueous solution) and for transport in blood plasma, xylem sap and phloem sap.

Describes a substance that is not attracted to water and does not dissolve in it because its molecules are non-polar, with no charges or significant partial charges. Lipids and the hydrocarbon tails of phospholipids are hydrophobic. Water does not repel such molecules: they are excluded because water molecules hydrogen-bond to each other more strongly than they are attracted to a non-polar molecule. The functions of some molecules depend on their being hydrophobic and insoluble, for example the phospholipid tails that form the core of membranes.

The upward force (upthrust) that a fluid exerts on a body immersed in it, equal to the weight of fluid displaced. Water is roughly 800 times denser than air, so it provides substantial support for the body of an aquatic animal such as a ringed seal, whereas air provides negligible support and an animal on land must bear its full weight through its skeleton and limbs.

The resistance of a fluid to flow, due to friction between its moving layers. Water is about 50 times more viscous than air, so an animal moving through water meets far more resistance than one moving through air; a streamlined shape, as in the ringed seal, reduces this resistance. Air's low viscosity offers little resistance to a bird in flight or to an animal walking on land.

A measure of how rapidly heat is conducted through a substance. Water conducts heat about 25 times faster than air, so an animal loses heat to water much faster than to air at the same temperature. Aquatic mammals such as the ringed seal have a thick layer of blubber as insulation, and a diving bird such as the black-throated loon relies on air trapped in its feathers.

The energy needed to raise the temperature of 1 kg of a substance by 1 K (1 °C). Water's specific heat capacity, about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, is roughly four times that of air per kilogram, and because water is also far denser, a body of water needs a very large energy input to change its temperature. Aquatic habitats therefore have stable temperatures that change slowly, whereas air temperature can change rapidly between day and night.

concepts.term: Black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) and ringed seal (Pusa hispida)
concepts.def: The guide's paired examples for contrasting water with air. The black-throated loon is a bird that flies through air, dives through water to catch fish, and comes ashore to nest; because air provides negligible upthrust, its wings must generate lift to support its full weight in flight and its skeleton and legs must bear it on land, while its wings meet little resistance in the low-viscosity air, and it loses heat much faster while diving than while flying. The ringed seal is an Arctic mammal that lives in water: upthrust supports most of its weight, its streamlined body reduces the resistance of viscous water, and a thick layer of blubber insulates it against rapid heat loss to the highly conductive water, whose temperature nonetheless stays stable because of water's high specific heat capacity. Either the common name or the scientific name may be used in an examination.

concepts.term: Asteroid hypothesis for the origin of Earth's water
concepts.def: The hypothesis that most of the water on Earth is of extraplanetary origin: it was delivered by asteroids containing water that collided with the early Earth. The abundance of water over the billions of years of Earth's history since then has allowed life to evolve.

Earth has kept its water for billions of years for two reasons: its gravity is strong enough to prevent water molecules in the atmosphere from escaping into space, and its surface temperatures are low enough for water vapour to condense, so most of the water is held as liquid in the oceans rather than as vapour that could be lost. A body with weak gravity, or one that is too hot for water to condense, cannot retain water.

The range of distances from a star within which the surface temperature of an orbiting planet could allow water to exist as a liquid: neither so close to the star that water would boil away nor so far that it would be permanently frozen (also called the habitable zone). Because life as we know it requires liquid water as its medium, the search for extraterrestrial life concentrates on planets within this zone. The distance of the zone from a star depends on how much energy the star emits, so it is not the same for every star.

mcqs.q: Water is described as the medium for life. What does this mean?
options: Most of the processes of life take place in aqueous solution.
Water is inert packing between the working parts of a cell.
Every substance that a cell uses must be dissolved in water.
Life processes occur in water only in aquatic organisms.
mcqs.specStatementText: Life happens in water: cells are aqueous, wherever they live
mcqs.explain: The first cells originated in water, and water remains the medium in which most processes of life occur: metabolic reactions happen in the aqueous cytoplasm and substances are transported dissolved in water.
rationales: The first cells originated in water, and water remains the medium in which most processes of life occur: metabolic reactions happen in the aqueous cytoplasm and substances are transported dissolved in water.
A student who sees water as passive packaging picks this. Water is not filler between the active parts: the aqueous cytoplasm is where most of the cell's reactions actually occur.
A student who thinks nothing useful can be insoluble picks this. Some molecules, such as the hydrophobic tails of membrane phospholipids, function precisely because they do not dissolve.
A student who confuses habitat with medium picks this. Land and flying organisms carry water inside their cells, and their metabolism still takes place in aqueous solution.

mcqs.q: Why is each covalent bond between oxygen and hydrogen in a water molecule polar?
options: Each hydrogen atom gives up its electron completely to the oxygen atom.
The shared electrons are drawn more strongly towards the oxygen atom.
It is a hydrogen bond, and hydrogen bonds are polar by their nature.
Oxygen and hydrogen atoms behave as opposite magnetic poles.
mcqs.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
mcqs.explain: Oxygen attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen does, so the electrons are shared unequally: oxygen becomes δ− and each hydrogen δ+. This unequal sharing is what makes the bond polar.
rationales: A student who treats the δ charges as full ionic charges picks this. In a polar covalent bond the electrons are shared unequally, not transferred; no ions form.

Oxygen attracts the shared electron pair more strongly than hydrogen does, so the electrons are shared unequally: oxygen becomes δ− and each hydrogen δ+. This unequal sharing is what makes the bond polar.
A student who thinks the bond inside the molecule is a hydrogen bond picks this. The O–H bond is a polar covalent bond; hydrogen bonds form between molecules because of that polarity.
A student who reads 'polar' as magnetic picks this. Polarity here is an uneven distribution of electric charge caused by unequal sharing of electrons, not magnetism.

mcqs.q: During transpiration, water molecules leave the liquid on the surface of a cell wall and enter the air. Which bonds are broken as each molecule leaves?
options: Polar covalent bonds between its oxygen and hydrogen atoms
Hydrogen bonds between the oxygen and hydrogens inside it
Hydrogen bonds between it and neighbouring molecules
Ionic bonds between its oxygen and hydrogen ions
mcqs.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
mcqs.explain: Hydrogen bonds link the δ+ hydrogens of one molecule to the δ− oxygens of its neighbours. These weak intermolecular bonds must be broken for the molecule to leave the liquid; the covalent bonds inside it are unaffected.
rationales: A student who thinks a physical change breaks the molecule apart picks this. Evaporation leaves both O–H covalent bonds intact; the molecule escapes whole.
A student who locates hydrogen bonds inside the molecule picks this. There are no hydrogen bonds within a water molecule; its internal bonds are polar covalent bonds, which do not break.

Hydrogen bonds link the δ+ hydrogens of one molecule to the δ− oxygens of its neighbours. These weak intermolecular bonds must be broken for the molecule to leave the liquid; the covalent bonds inside it are unaffected.
A student who reads δ+ and δ− as full charges picks this. Water is not made of ions; the partial charges give rise to hydrogen bonds, not ionic bonds.

mcqs.q: Transpiration puts the column of water in a xylem vessel under tension. Why does the column not break as it is pulled upwards?
options: Root pressure pushes the column upwards from below.
Capillary action lifts the water inside the narrow vessel.
Hydrogen bonds within each molecule resist the pull.
Hydrogen bonds hold the molecules to each other.
mcqs.explain: Cohesion due to hydrogen bonding keeps the water molecules attached to one another, so the tension created by evaporation in the leaves is transmitted down the whole column and water is drawn up without the column separating.
rationales: A student who thinks water is pushed up from the roots picks this. The column in a transpiring plant is pulled from above and is under tension; what stops it breaking is the attraction between the water molecules.
A student who thinks capillary rise carries water up the whole plant picks this. Capillary action moves water only short distances; the column is held together under tension by cohesion.

A student who locates hydrogen bonds inside the water molecule picks this. The bonds within a molecule are polar covalent bonds; the hydrogen bonds that keep the column continuous are between neighbouring molecules.

Cohesion due to hydrogen bonding keeps the water molecules attached to one another, so the tension created by evaporation in the leaves is transmitted down the whole column and water is drawn up without the column separating.

mcqs.q: A pond skater rests on a pond. Its legs make small dents in the water surface but do not pass through it. What allows the surface to support the insect?
options: Cohesion between surface molecules makes the surface act like an elastic film.
The insect is less dense than water, so upthrust holds it at the surface.
Water adheres to the insect's legs and so holds them up on the surface.
The strong hydrogen bonds at the surface form a rigid, solid-like layer.
mcqs.explain: Molecules at the surface are held to their neighbours by hydrogen bonds and resist being separated, so the surface behaves like a stretched film. This surface tension, a consequence of cohesion, lets small animals use the water surface as a habitat.
rationales: Molecules at the surface are held to their neighbours by hydrogen bonds and resist being separated, so the surface behaves like a stretched film. This surface tension, a consequence of cohesion, lets small animals use the water surface as a habitat.

A student who treats the insect as a floating object picks this. A pond skater is denser than water and sinks if its legs pass through the surface; it is supported by surface tension, not by upthrust.
A student who thinks water sticks to any surface picks this. The legs are water-repellent; if water adhered to them they would be wetted and pulled through the surface.
A student who thinks hydrogen bonds are strong and permanent picks this. Individual hydrogen bonds are weak and constantly re-forming; the surface is a flexible film that dents, not a rigid layer.

mcqs.q: Water rises through the narrow spaces between soil particles, against gravity. Which explanation of this movement is correct?
options: Cohesion between the water and the soil particles draws the water upwards.
Water adheres to the polar or charged surfaces of the soil particles.
Water adheres to any solid surface, whatever the surface is made of.
Air pressure in the soil pushes the water up into the spaces.
mcqs.specStatementText: Adhesion: water sticks to polar or charged surfaces
mcqs.explain: Soil particle surfaces are polar or charged, so water molecules are attracted to them (adhesion). Together with cohesion between water molecules, this pulls water through the narrow spaces: capillary action.
rationales: A student who uses 'cohesion' for any sticking that water does picks this. Attraction between water and a different material is adhesion; cohesion is the attraction between water molecules.

Soil particle surfaces are polar or charged, so water molecules are attracted to them (adhesion). Together with cohesion between water molecules, this pulls water through the narrow spaces: capillary action.
A student who thinks water sticks to everything picks this. Adhesion needs a polar or charged surface; water does not adhere to non-polar surfaces such as wax.
A student who explains capillary rise by suction or pressure picks this. No external pressure is involved; the rise is caused by adhesion to the particle surfaces combined with cohesion.

mcqs.q: In a leaf, water evaporates from the cellulose cell walls of spongy mesophyll cells. How does adhesion contribute to water transport?
options: It pushes water out of the xylem into the cell walls under root pressure.
It holds water against the waxy cuticle so that less of it evaporates.
It draws water into the cell walls to replace water that evaporates.
It alone lifts water the whole way from the roots up to the leaf.
mcqs.specStatementText: Adhesion: water sticks to polar or charged surfaces
mcqs.explain: Water adheres to the polar cellulose of the cell walls, so as water evaporates it is replaced by water drawn through the walls by capillary action. This pull is transmitted to the xylem, generating the tension that moves water up the plant.
rationales: A student who thinks water is pushed from the roots picks this. Adhesion pulls water into the cell walls; it does not push, and root pressure is not the force involved in a transpiring leaf.
A student who thinks water adheres to any surface picks this. Wax is non-polar, so water does not adhere to the cuticle; adhesion acts on the polar cellulose of cell walls.

Water adheres to the polar cellulose of the cell walls, so as water evaporates it is replaced by water drawn through the walls by capillary action. This pull is transmitted to the xylem, generating the tension that moves water up the plant.

A student who believes capillary action moves water up the whole plant picks this. Adhesion acts in the cell walls over short distances; long-distance transport is by tension transmitted through the cohesive water column.

mcqs.q: Why do so many different substances dissolve in water?
options: Water splits every solute into positive and negative ions.
Water breaks the covalent bonds within the solute molecules.
Water molecules are magnetic and so attract other substances.
Polar water molecules attract polar and charged solutes.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
mcqs.explain: The δ+ and δ− regions of water molecules are attracted to charged particles and to the polar groups of molecules, so a wide variety of hydrophilic substances dissolve. This is why water is the medium for metabolism and transport.
rationales: A student who thinks dissolving always means forming ions picks this. Ionic compounds do separate into ions, but polar molecules such as glucose dissolve intact by hydrogen bonding to water.
A student who thinks dissolving is a chemical breakdown picks this. Dissolving is a physical change: the solute's molecules stay whole and become surrounded by water molecules.
A student who reads 'polar' as magnetic picks this. Water's polarity is an uneven distribution of electric charge, and it attracts solutes electrically, not magnetically.

The δ+ and δ− regions of water molecules are attracted to charged particles and to the polar groups of molecules, so a wide variety of hydrophilic substances dissolve. This is why water is the medium for metabolism and transport.

mcqs.q: Which statement about the hydrophobic hydrocarbon tails of the phospholipids in a cell membrane is correct?
options: Their insolubility in water is what holds the bilayer together as a barrier.
Their insolubility means that they have no function in the membrane.
They are pushed away from water by a repulsive force from water molecules.
They are insoluble because they contain no ions that water can separate.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
mcqs.explain: Because the tails are non-polar and insoluble, they are excluded from water and cluster together in the centre of the bilayer, with the hydrophilic heads facing the water. The membrane's function depends on the tails being hydrophobic.
rationales: Because the tails are non-polar and insoluble, they are excluded from water and cluster together in the centre of the bilayer, with the hydrophilic heads facing the water. The membrane's function depends on the tails being hydrophobic.
A student who thinks only dissolved molecules can be useful picks this. The function of some molecules depends on them being hydrophobic and insoluble; the tails form the membrane's core.
A student who takes 'hydrophobic' to mean actively repelled picks this. There is no repulsion; water molecules attract each other more strongly than they attract the tails, so the tails are excluded.
A student who thinks only ionic substances dissolve picks this. Glucose contains no ions yet dissolves; the tails are insoluble because they are non-polar and cannot form hydrogen bonds with water.

mcqs.q: Glucose is carried dissolved in blood plasma and in phloem sap, and it is broken down by enzymes in the aqueous cytoplasm. Which property of glucose makes this possible?
options: It separates into positive and negative ions in water.
Its many hydroxyl (–OH) groups form hydrogen bonds with water.
It is a small molecule, and small molecules dissolve readily.
Water breaks its covalent bonds, splitting it into soluble fragments.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
mcqs.explain: The polar –OH groups of glucose hydrogen-bond with water molecules, so glucose is hydrophilic and dissolves. Dissolved glucose can be transported in plasma and phloem sap and acted on by enzymes in aqueous solution.
rationales: A student who thinks dissolving means forming ions picks this. Glucose is a covalent molecule and does not ionise; it dissolves because it is polar.

The polar –OH groups of glucose hydrogen-bond with water molecules, so glucose is hydrophilic and dissolves. Dissolved glucose can be transported in plasma and phloem sap and acted on by enzymes in aqueous solution.
A student who equates small with soluble picks this. Solubility depends on polarity, not size: large polar proteins dissolve, while small non-polar molecules do not.
A student who thinks dissolving breaks molecules apart picks this. Dissolving is a physical change; a glucose molecule stays whole and is surrounded by water molecules.

mcqs.q: Which statement correctly describes a consequence of the physical properties of water for a ringed seal (Pusa hispida)?
options: Because it can sink, the water gives its body no support.
It loses heat slowly because water is a poor conductor of heat.
Upthrust from the sea water supports most of its body weight.
The sea stays warm because of water's high specific heat capacity.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
mcqs.explain: Water is dense, so the upthrust on the seal's body is close to its weight (buoyancy). The seal needs far less skeletal support than a land animal, which receives negligible upthrust from air.
rationales: A student who thinks upthrust acts only on floating objects picks this. Upthrust acts on any immersed body; the seal's density is close to that of water, so most of its weight is supported.
A student who merges specific heat capacity with conductivity picks this. Water conducts heat about 25 times faster than air, so the seal loses heat rapidly and needs thick blubber.
Water is dense, so the upthrust on the seal's body is close to its weight (buoyancy). The seal needs far less skeletal support than a land animal, which receives negligible upthrust from air.
A student who reads 'high heat capacity' as 'warm' picks this. High specific heat capacity makes the sea's temperature stable, not warm; Arctic sea water is close to 0 °C.

mcqs.q: Thermal conductivity: water 0.60 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, air 0.025 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹. Specific heat capacity: water 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, air 1000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹. A ringed seal in sea water at 5 °C and a black-throated loon standing in air at 5 °C have the same body temperature. Other factors being equal, which conclusion is justified?
options: Heat is conducted away from the seal's skin only about 4 times faster.
The seal loses less heat, because water stores much more heat than air.
The seal is in colder surroundings, since water at 5 °C is colder than air at 5 °C.
Heat is conducted away from the seal's skin about 24 times faster.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
mcqs.explain: Rate of conduction is proportional to thermal conductivity, other factors being equal: 0.60 / 0.025 = 24. This is why a seal needs thick blubber in water no colder than the air the loon stands in.
rationales: A student who confuses the two properties uses the specific heat capacity ratio (4200 / 1000 ≈ 4). The rate of conduction depends on thermal conductivity, and 0.60 / 0.025 = 24.
A student who reads heat capacity as a store of warmth picks this. Water's high specific heat capacity keeps its temperature stable; it does not reduce the rate at which heat leaves the seal.
A student who judges temperature by how cold something feels picks this. Both are at 5 °C; water feels colder only because it conducts heat away from the skin much faster.
Rate of conduction is proportional to thermal conductivity, other factors being equal: 0.60 / 0.025 = 24. This is why a seal needs thick blubber in water no colder than the air the loon stands in.

mcqs.q: A black-throated loon (Gavia arctica) flies through air and dives through water. Which statement about these two fluids is correct?
options: Water is far more viscous than air, so it resists the loon's movement much more.
Air has no viscosity, so the loon meets no resistance when it flies.
Water conducts heat more slowly than air, so the loon cools less when diving.
Water stores more heat than air, so the loon is kept warmer while it dives.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
mcqs.explain: Water's viscosity is about 50 times that of air, so a diving loon meets far greater resistance than a flying one. Animals that move through water benefit from streamlining for this reason.
rationales: Water's viscosity is about 50 times that of air, so a diving loon meets far greater resistance than a flying one. Animals that move through water benefit from streamlining for this reason.
A student who thinks only liquids are viscous picks this. Air does have viscosity, though it is low, so flight meets some resistance; it is simply far less than in water.
A student who merges heat capacity with conductivity picks this. Water conducts heat about 25 times faster than air, so the loon loses heat far more quickly while diving.
A student who reads high heat capacity as warmth picks this. Water's high specific heat capacity stabilises its temperature; it does not warm the loon, which loses heat faster in water.

mcqs.q: The Moon formed close to Earth and was struck by the same water-bearing asteroids, yet its surface has almost no water today. Which explanation is correct?
options: It has no ozone layer to act as a lid that keeps water vapour in.
Its gravity is too weak to hold water vapour, which escapes to space.
It had no volcanoes to release water made from rock in its interior.
It lies outside the Goldilocks zone, so any water froze or boiled off.
mcqs.specStatementText: Where Earth's water came from, and why it stayed
mcqs.explain: Retention of water depends on gravity strong enough to hold water molecules and on temperatures low enough for water to condense. The Moon's small mass gives it gravity too weak to retain water vapour, so water delivered by asteroids was lost.
rationales: A student who pictures the atmosphere as a lid picks this. No layer seals water in; it is gravity that retains water molecules, and the Moon's gravity is too weak to do so.

Retention of water depends on gravity strong enough to hold water molecules and on temperatures low enough for water to condense. The Moon's small mass gives it gravity too weak to retain water vapour, so water delivered by asteroids was lost.
A student who thinks water is made inside a planet picks this. Water is not made from rock; the hypothesis studied is that water was delivered by asteroids, and the Moon received them too.
A student who equates the zone with having water picks this. The Moon orbits the Sun at the same distance as Earth and is inside the zone; being there does not guarantee water.

mcqs.q: Where is most of the water on Earth thought to have come from?
options: From hydrogen and oxygen gases that reacted in the early atmosphere
From water formed inside the Earth and released by volcanoes
From water-bearing asteroids that collided with the early Earth
From nowhere: planets in the Goldilocks zone are bound to hold liquid water
mcqs.specStatementText: Where Earth's water came from, and why it stayed
mcqs.explain: The hypothesis in the guide is that Earth's water is of extraplanetary origin, delivered by water-bearing asteroids that struck the early Earth. Its abundance since then has allowed life to evolve.
rationales: A student who remembers hydrogen burning in oxygen picks this. The early atmosphere did not contain free hydrogen and oxygen in the amounts needed; the hypothesis studied is extraplanetary delivery.
A student who recalls the GCSE story of volcanic outgassing picks this. Volcanoes moved water to the surface but did not make it; the water itself is thought to have arrived from beyond the planet.
The hypothesis in the guide is that Earth's water is of extraplanetary origin, delivered by water-bearing asteroids that struck the early Earth. Its abundance since then has allowed life to evolve.

A student who thinks being in the Goldilocks zone guarantees water picks this. The zone only means temperatures could allow liquid water to persist; it does not supply water, which is thought to have been delivered by asteroids.

mcqs.q: Astronomers find a rocky planet orbiting within the Goldilocks zone of its star. Which conclusion is justified?
options: Liquid water and living organisms must both exist on the planet's surface.
It orbits at the same distance from its star as Earth does from the Sun.
Any water there, whether ice, liquid or vapour, would support life equally.
Liquid water could exist on its surface, so it is worth investigating.
mcqs.specStatementText: Looking for life means looking for liquid water
mcqs.explain: The Goldilocks zone is the range of distances at which surface temperatures could allow liquid water. That makes the planet a candidate for the search for life, but the presence of water and of life must be established separately.
rationales: A student who treats the zone as proof of life picks this. The zone only means temperatures could allow liquid water; the Moon is in the Sun's zone yet has no liquid surface water and no life.
A student who thinks the zone is a fixed distance picks this. The zone depends on the star's energy output; around a dim star it is much closer in, around a bright star further out.
A student who counts water in any state picks this. Life needs liquid water as its medium for dissolving, transporting and reacting; ice and vapour cannot serve.

The Goldilocks zone is the range of distances at which surface temperatures could allow liquid water. That makes the planet a candidate for the search for life, but the presence of water and of life must be established separately.

mcqs.q: Over a clear spring day and night, the air above a lake varies between 2 °C and 18 °C, but the lake water 1 m below the surface stays between 7 °C and 8 °C. Which explanation of the stable water temperature is correct?
options: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so a large energy input or loss is needed to change its temperature.
Water has a high thermal conductivity, so heat passes through it too quickly to change its temperature.
Water stores a large amount of heat, so the lake is warmer than the air above it throughout the day.
Energy supplied to the water is used to break the covalent bonds inside its molecules rather than to raise its temperature.
mcqs.specStatementText: Water's physical properties shape life in it
mcqs.explain: Water's specific heat capacity is about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, roughly four times that of air per kilogram, and the lake also has a very large mass, so the energy gained by day and lost by night changes its temperature only slightly. This stability of temperature is a consequence of water's high specific heat capacity for animals in aquatic habitats.
rationales: Water's specific heat capacity is about 4200 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹, roughly four times that of air per kilogram, and the lake also has a very large mass, so the energy gained by day and lost by night changes its temperature only slightly. This stability of temperature is a consequence of water's high specific heat capacity for animals in aquatic habitats.

A student who merges thermal conductivity with specific heat capacity picks this. Thermal conductivity describes how fast heat passes through water, not how much its temperature changes; it is the high specific heat capacity that makes a large energy change produce only a small temperature change.

A student who reads high heat capacity as warmth picks this. The data show the air reaching 18 °C by day while the lake stays at 7 °C to 8 °C, so the lake is not warmer; high specific heat capacity makes the temperature stable, not high.

A student who thinks supplying energy to water breaks its molecules apart picks this. Warming the lake is a physical change and the O–H covalent bonds stay intact; the energy raises the temperature, but a very large amount is needed because of water's high specific heat capacity.

mcqs.q: Two water molecules are drawn using the notation for polarity and hydrogen bonding. Which feature of the drawing is correct?
options: A dashed line joins the oxygen to one of the two hydrogens within the same water molecule.
A dashed line joins a hydrogen labelled δ+ on one molecule to the oxygen labelled δ− on the other.
The oxygen is labelled with a full − and each hydrogen with a full +, because the molecule is made of ions.
A solid line joins the two molecules, because the bond between them is as strong as a covalent bond.
mcqs.specStatementText: Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
mcqs.explain: The δ− is written beside the oxygen and δ+ beside each hydrogen, because the shared electrons are drawn towards the oxygen. A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, shown as a dashed line from the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule to the δ− oxygen of its neighbour.
rationales: A student who locates hydrogen bonds inside the water molecule picks this. The line between an oxygen and a hydrogen of the same molecule is a solid line for a polar covalent bond; the dashed hydrogen bond always runs between two different molecules.

The δ− is written beside the oxygen and δ+ beside each hydrogen, because the shared electrons are drawn towards the oxygen. A hydrogen bond is an attraction between molecules, shown as a dashed line from the δ+ hydrogen of one molecule to the δ− oxygen of its neighbour.

A student who reads the δ symbols as full ionic charges picks this. The δ indicates a partial charge from unequal sharing of electrons; no electron is transferred, so water contains no ions and the labels are δ+ and δ−, not + and −.

A student who thinks hydrogen bonds are as strong as covalent bonds picks this. The bond between molecules is a hydrogen bond, much weaker than a covalent bond and continually breaking and re-forming, which is why it is drawn as a dashed rather than a solid line.

specSource: IB Diploma Programme Biology (guide first assessment 2025); topic A1.1 Water

specStatements.text: Life happens in water: cells are aqueous, wherever they live
Polar bonds inside the molecule; hydrogen bonds between molecules
Adhesion: water sticks to polar or charged surfaces
Water is the solvent for metabolism and transport
Water's physical properties shape life in it
Where Earth's water came from, and why it stayed
Looking for life means looking for liquid water

scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the asteroid-delivery hypothesis is presented for the origin of Earth's water; comets, the solar nebula and water held in the mantle are not mentioned, and no isotope-ratio evidence is used. Retention is explained only by Earth's gravity and by surface temperatures low enough for water to condense; the magnetic field, solar wind stripping and photodissociation are not included.
